A.explanation: This uses the horizontal component $T\cos 20^{\circ}$ instead of the vertical component to balance the weight, giving $T = mg/(2\cos 20^{\circ})$.

B.explanation: This is close to the weight $mg \approx 0.83\text{ kN}$, so it ignores that only the small vertical part $T\sin 20^{\circ}$ of each tension supports the man.

D.explanation: This uses only one wire, $T\sin 20^{\circ} = mg$, missing the factor of 2 for the two sides and giving twice the correct tension.

hints: Notice the 85 kg man is at rest at the midpoint, so his downward weight $W = mg$ must be balanced by upward forces from the two equal tensions $T$.
Each wire is at $20^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, so resolve $T$ into vertical and horizontal parts and identify which part, $T\sin 20^{\circ}$ or $T\cos 20^{\circ}$, acts upward.
Add the upward components from both left and right wires, set the sum equal to $85 \times 9.81\text{ N}$, and solve for $T$ before converting to $\text{kN}$.
walkthrough: Calculate the weight of the man: $W = mg = 85 \times 9.81 = 834\text{ N}$ downward.
Resolve one tension: with $20^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, the vertical upward component is $T\sin 20^{\circ}$ and the horizontal component is $T\cos 20^{\circ}$.
Apply vertical equilibrium for the point where the man stands: the two symmetric upward components balance the weight, so $T\sin 20^{\circ} + T\sin 20^{\circ} = W$.
Convert to kilonewtons: $1220\text{ N} \approx 1.2\text{ kN}$. This is option C.
